---
title: Introduction
description: Git shows what changed. Entire shows why.
---

Entire is a CLI-first system of record that captures the context behind agent-assisted code changes and links it to Git.

## Why Entire exists

When an agent changes code, the final diff leaves out important context:

- The prompt that started the work
- Files the agent inspected
- Tools it ran
- Decisions it made
- [Checkpoints](/guides/checkpoints/overview) it created along the way

Entire records that context so teams can review, search, and continue agent work with the same confidence they expect from Git history.

## What Entire helps you do

- Review the prompt, transcript, and tool calls behind a commit, not just the diff.
- Browse Checkpoints from an agent session as the work evolves.
- Search prompts, sessions, and repository history.
- Continue from prior agent work instead of starting cold.
- Share agent context with teammates through Git-linked history.

## How it works

1. Install the Entire CLI in your repository.
2. Connect Entire to the coding agent you use.
3. Entire captures sessions and Checkpoints as the agent works.
4. Use the CLI or Entire.io to inspect the history behind commits.

## Start here

Choose the fastest path for what you need next.

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Quickstart" icon="rocket" href="/quickstart">
    Set up Entire and capture your first agent session.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Installation" icon="download" href="/installation">
    Install the Entire CLI.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Agents" icon="robot" href="/agents/overview">
    Connect Entire to your coding agent.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Checkpoints" icon="flag" href="/guides/checkpoints/overview">
    Learn how Entire records agent-assisted changes.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>
---
title: Quickstart
description: Get started with Entire by creating your first checkpoint.
---

This quickstart walks you from installing Entire to creating your first checkpoint: a record of the prompts, transcript, tool calls, and file changes behind an AI-assisted commit.

## Prerequisites

- Git installed and configured
- An AI coding agent installed, such as Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Factory, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or Pi
- macOS, Linux, or Windows
- Optional: GitHub CLI (`gh`) installed and authenticated, if you want Entire to create and push a private GitHub repository during setup

## 1. Install Entire

Entire ships two release channels:

- `stable`: recommended for most users.
- `nightly`: prerelease builds with newer changes.

Nightly is available through Homebrew and the Linux install script. Scoop currently supports stable only.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="macOS (Homebrew)">
    ```bash
    # One-time setup: tap and trust
    brew tap entireio/tap
    brew trust entireio/tap

    # Stable
    brew install --cask entire

    # Nightly
    brew install --cask entire@nightly
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Linux">
    ```bash
    # Stable
    curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash

    # Nightly
    curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Windows (Scoop)">
    ```bash
    scoop bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git
    scoop install entire/cli
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="From Source">
    ```bash
    go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Verify the installation:

```bash
entire version
```

## 2. Create a Demo Project

```bash
mkdir entire-demo
cd entire-demo
```

<Note>
Already in a Git repository? Skip this step and run the remaining commands from the repository root.
</Note>

## 3. Enable Entire

Choose the agent you already use, then run its setup command.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Claude Code">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent claude-code
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Codex">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent codex
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Copilot CLI">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent copilot-cli
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Cursor">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent cursor
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Factory">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent factoryai-droid
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Gemini CLI">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent gemini
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="OpenCode">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent opencode
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Pi">
    ```bash
    entire enable -y --agent pi
    ```
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

This installs Git hooks that capture checkpoints when you commit and installs hook configuration for your selected agent. It also creates a `.entire/` directory for project and local settings.

For shared projects, commit `.entire/settings.json` and `.entire/.gitignore`. Keep `.entire/settings.local.json` local for personal overrides.

<Note>
Because this starts in a new folder, `entire enable -y` initializes Git and creates an initial commit. If `gh` is installed and authenticated, Entire can also create a private GitHub repository and push the initial commit.
</Note>

## 4. Start an Agent Session

Start the same agent you enabled:

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Claude Code">
    ```bash
    claude
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Codex">
    ```bash
    codex
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Copilot CLI">
    ```bash
    copilot
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Cursor">
    ```bash
    cursor
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Factory">
    ```bash
    droid
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Gemini CLI">
    ```bash
    gemini
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="OpenCode">
    ```bash
    opencode
    ```
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Pi">
    ```bash
    pi
    ```
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

Prompt it to make a small change:

```text
Create a file named hello-entire.md with a short note explaining that this repo is my first Entire checkpoint demo.
```

When the agent finishes, exit the agent session if needed.

## 5. Commit the Change

Check what changed:

```bash
git status
```

Then commit it:

```bash
git add hello-entire.md
git commit -m "Add first Entire demo file"
```

Because Entire detected recent agent work, it may ask whether to link this commit to the session context. The agent name will match the integration you enabled:

```text
Entire: Active <agent> session detected
  Last prompt: Create a file named hello-entire.md with a short note...

Link this commit to session context?
  [Y]es / [n]o / [a]lways (remember my choice):
```

Press `Enter` or type `y` to link the commit. After the commit succeeds, you have created your first checkpoint.

<Note>
If you choose `always`, Entire remembers that preference and links future matching commits automatically.
</Note>

## 6. View Your First Checkpoint

```bash
entire checkpoint list
```

You should see the checkpoint linked to your commit.

Entire stores permanent checkpoint data on a Git branch named:

```text
entire/checkpoints/v1
```

Your working branch stays clean. Entire does not add extra commits to it.

## 7. Optional: Push Your Code and Checkpoint

If your repository has a remote, push your code:

```bash
git push
```

Entire's pre-push hook also syncs checkpoint data to `entire/checkpoints/v1`.

<Note>
Checkpoint data can include session context. If your repository is public, pushed checkpoint history is public too. See [Security & Privacy](/security) and [Checkpoint Remote](/guides/configuration/checkpoint-storage#checkpoint-remote).
</Note>

## What's Next?

---
title: Overview
sidebarTitle: Overview
description: Give your agent a map of your codebase so it finds the right code before it starts editing.
---

Entire Graph is a plugin for the [Entire CLI](/platforms/cli). It builds a local map of one repository: every function, type, and the calls between them. Your coding agent can then look code up instead of hunting for it.

Without it, an agent starting a task greps for a likely name, reads a few whole files, guesses, and greps again. That is slow, it burns context, and it misses things. With Graph installed, the agent's first move is a single ranked query that returns `file:line` locations, and it reads only what those results point at.

## Why teams turn it on

- **Agents find the right file first.** One ranked query replaces a round of grep-and-read.
- **You see the blast radius before you change something.** Graph reports callers, callees, type consumers, and files that historically change together.
- **It stays on your machine.** The analyzer parses your repository locally with tree-sitter. It makes no network requests, no model calls, and no API-key lookups.
- **Results are reproducible.** The same repository and the same options produce the same answer, so a surprising result can be audited instead of re-rolled.

## How it differs from `entire search`

Entire ships two things called search. They answer different questions.

| | [`entire search`](/cli-reference/search) | `entire graph search` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answers | Who worked on this, and why does it exist? | Where is this code, and what touches it? |
| Looks at | Checkpoints, sessions, commits, indexed code | The structure of one repository's source |
| Scope | Every repository your account can reach | The repository you are standing in |
| Runs | Against Entire.io | Entirely on your machine |
| Needs login | Yes | No |

Use `entire search` to recover history. Use `entire graph search` to locate code. Most sessions use both: find the code, then find out why it looks the way it does.

## Set up Graph

Graph needs Entire CLI 0.10.0 or later. Check with `entire version`, and [update](/updating) if you are behind.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Install the plugin">
    ```bash
    entire plugin install graph
    ```

    Confirm it is on the path:

    ```bash
    entire graph version
    ```

    You should see a release tag such as `v0.4.0`. A build that prints `dev` is an unversioned local build.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Turn it on for a repository">
    From the repository root:

    ```bash
    entire graph init-agents --repo .
    ```

    This writes three files:

    - `.entire/graph-agent.md`: the instructions your agent follows. Regenerated in full on every run, so edits here do not survive.
    - `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`: created if missing. Otherwise one managed block between `<!-- entire-graph:begin -->` and `<!-- entire-graph:end -->` is added or replaced. Everything outside those markers is left alone.

    Review the three files and commit them together so the instructions apply to your whole team.

    <Note>
    Committing also matters for speed. All three files are indexable Markdown, and Graph turns off cache reuse while the working tree is dirty. Leave them uncommitted and every query rebuilds the index from scratch.
    </Note>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Start a fresh agent session">
    A session that was already open has not read the new instructions. Quit it and start again in the repository.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Ask your first question

You do not run Graph commands yourself. You ask your agent a question in plain language, and it runs the queries.

```text
Without changing any files, find where route matching is implemented,
what calls it, and what breaks if its behavior changes.
```

A correctly activated agent answers that by running `entire graph search` first, then `entire graph impact`, then reading narrow line ranges around the locations those returned. Its answer cites files and lines it actually opened.

Running `impact` directly shows the kind of evidence it gets back:

```text
Index: cache-miss (807ms) | Query: 0ms | Total: 807ms
Impact: Router.Match (mux.go:151) def=151 span=151-182 [method in Router]
Blast radius: 1 caller (1 direct, 0 transitive), 0 callees, 3 type consumers,
  1 data flow, 7 co-change files, 29 siblings.
Callers (1 direct, 0 transitive; who breaks if behavior changes):
- Router.ServeHTTP (mux.go:203, def :188)
```

Ask the same question again and the first line reads `cache-hit`, in a fraction of the time.

## What your agent runs underneath

Prompts are the interface. These are the commands behind them, and you can run any of them yourself for manual inspection or scripting.

| What you want | What you ask | What runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Find the implementation | Find where request routing is implemented. | `search` |
| Read one definition | Show me the definition of `RouteMatch`. | `def` |
| Trace callers | What calls `Router.Match`? | `neighbors` |
| Check the blast radius | What would changing `Router.Match` affect? | `impact` |
| Review a branch | Summarize the semantic changes from `main` to `HEAD`. | `diff` |

See [Graph Commands](/guides/graph/commands) for the full surface and the defaults that matter.

## Check that it is working

Each layer of the setup has something you can look at:

1. **Installed.** `entire version` and `entire graph version` both succeed.
2. **Turned on.** The three files exist, each with one intact marker pair.
3. **Adopted.** In a fresh session, the agent's first code-locating call is `entire graph search`, not a broad grep or a whole-file read. If it starts elsewhere, the guide probably did not load.
4. **Grounded.** The answer cites files and lines the agent opened after the query.

## What Graph does not do

Graph is code intelligence for one repository. It does not store conversation or user memory, run in the background, or expose its own MCP server. That is [Checkpoints](/guides/checkpoints/overview) and [Sessions](/guides/sessions/overview) territory.

Static analysis is also a best effort, not a compiler. Calls through interfaces, reflection, dynamic dispatch, and generated code can be missed or left unresolved, so dependent counts are a guide for inspection rather than a guarantee. Files the parser cannot handle are reported as partial failures rather than dropped silently.

Coverage comes in two tiers: 36 languages get full semantic parsing, and another 149 filetypes get file and symbol structure without call or type analysis. Check what your build supports with `entire graph capabilities --json`.

## Continue with

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Set Up Graph" icon="wrench" href="/guides/graph/set-up-graph">
    Install the plugin and turn it on for a repository.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Graph Commands" icon="terminal" href="/guides/graph/commands">
    Every query, analysis, and export command.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Graph Troubleshooting" icon="stethoscope" href="/guides/graph/troubleshooting">
    Fix install, adoption, and cache problems.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Search" icon="magnifying-glass" href="/guides/search/overview">
    Find past agent work and its context across repositories.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

title: Graph Commands
sidebarTitle: Commands
description: Every Graph command, grouped by task, with the defaults that matter most.
---

Day to day, your agent drives Graph by following the guide that `init-agents` installs. The same commands are available to you directly, for manual inspection, for checking a result your agent acted on, or for scripting.

```bash
entire graph COMMAND [flags]
```

Run `entire graph help` to see every command in your installed version, and `entire graph COMMAND --help` for its flags. Those are authoritative. This page groups the commands by what you are trying to do.

Pass `--repo .` when you run these outside an Entire session.

## Which tree each command reads

This trips people up, so it is worth learning once.

| Command family | Reads by default | Switch with |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| Queries: `search`, `def`, `explain`, `neighbors`, `impact` | Your working tree, so uncommitted edits are visible | `--head` for the committed tree |
| Streams: `snapshot`, `symbols`, `edges` | The committed tree | `--worktree` |
| Change analysis: `diff`, `commit`, `checkpoint` | Committed refs | Not applicable |

## Set up

| Command | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `init-agents` | Writes `.entire/graph-agent.md` and managed blocks in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. See [Set Up Graph](/guides/graph/set-up-graph). |
| `agent-guide` | Prints the guide `init-agents` installs, so you can read it or pipe it elsewhere. |
| `index` | Prebuilds a committed-tree cache before a batch of `--head` queries. Defaults to `--profile full`. |
| `capabilities` | Reports which languages are semantically parsed, which are inventory only, plus relation types and features. Requires `--json`. |

## Find and understand code

These five are the interactive query family.

### search

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description of a task or bug. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "token refresh returns 401"
```

Results are byte-budgeted to drop straight into an agent's context. Top hits come back as full function bodies, later hits shrink to locators, and `--max-context-bytes` bounds the total.

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--query TEXT` | The task or bug in one plain sentence. Required. |
| `--top-k N` | Number of results. Default is `10`. |
| `--format text\|json\|ndjson\|agent` | Default is `json`. `text` is tiered for reading, `agent` is compact. |
| `--profile syntax-only\|fast\|full` | Parsing depth. Default is `fast`, but the installed agent guide asks for `full`, which activates the call graph. |
| `--deep` | Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it in. Slower, and reads every eligible file. |
| `--head` | Search the committed tree instead of the working tree. |
| `--max-context-bytes N` | Output byte budget. `0` removes the bound. Default is `24576`. |

Each result carries a `signals` array naming why it ranked, such as `path`, `body`, `symbol-name`, or `graph:callers`, so a surprising hit can be audited instead of trusted.

### impact

Everything the graph knows about changing one symbol, in one bounded answer. Run this before changing a function or type's behavior.

```bash
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol Router.Match
```

```text
Index: cache-hit (64ms) | Query: 0ms | Total: 64ms
Impact: Router.Match (mux.go:151) def=151 span=151-182 [method in Router]
Blast radius: 1 caller (1 direct, 0 transitive), 0 callees, 3 type consumers,
  1 data flow, 7 co-change files, 29 siblings.
Callers (1 direct, 0 transitive; who breaks if behavior changes):
- Router.ServeHTTP (mux.go:203, def :188)
```

You get direct and transitive callers up to depth 2, callees, type consumers, data flows, files that historically change alongside this one, and same-container siblings.

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--symbol NAME\|FILE:LINE` | Symbol to analyze. Required. |
| `--depth 1\|2` | Caller traversal depth. Default is `2`. |
| `--limit N` | Max entries per section. Default is `15`. |
| `--exclude-tests` | Drop test-only entries. |
| `--file`, `--line`, `--kind` | Disambiguate an ambiguous name. |

### neighbors

Direct relations for one symbol, when you want a specific relation and direction rather than the full blast radius.

```bash
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol validateToken --relation CALLS --direction in
```

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--symbol NAME\|FILE:LINE` | Symbol to inspect. Required. |
| `--relation TYPE` | Relation family to follow. Default is `CALLS`. |
| `--direction both\|in\|out` | `in` is callers, `out` is callees. Default is `both`. |
| `--depth 1\|2` | Hops to traverse. Default is `1`. |
| `--limit N` | Max neighbors per direction. Default is `20`. |
| `--internal-only` | Drop unresolved external endpoints. |

### def

What a name is: its declaration, and for a type, its fields and method surface.

```bash
entire graph def RouteMatch --repo .
```

Membership comes from the graph's own edges, never from one name resembling another. For an interface, it reports who implements it.

### explain

Resolves the symbols named by a failing build or test. It reads the failure from stdin.

```bash
go test ./... 2>&1 | entire graph explain --repo .
```

By default it echoes the input through and appends declarations for the symbols the failure named, resolved against the working tree so they match the code that just failed.

## Analyze changes

| Command | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `commit [REV]` | Entity-level change list for a commit against its first parent: added, removed, renamed, signature-changed, body-changed, each with a heuristic dependent count. |
| `diff --base A --head B` | The same, between two refs. `analyze` is an alias. |
| `checkpoint ID` | Runs that analysis on the commit behind an [Entire-Checkpoint](/guides/checkpoints/overview) trailer. Useful when deciding whether a checkpoint is safe to keep, revert, or continue. |
| `verify --test "CMD"` | Runs your test command and reports which tests changed state, rather than forwarding runner output. |

A high dependent count on a signature change is the signal to run tests first.

<Warning>
`entire graph verify` executes the command you give it, with your privileges. So does `--setup`. Pass only commands you would run yourself.
</Warning>

`verify` is more useful with a baseline. Record one on a clean tree, then compare after editing, so a failure that predated your change gets labelled `PRE-EXISTING` instead of blamed on you:

```bash
entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/" --record-baseline /tmp/base.json
# make your edit
entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/" --pre-edit-baseline /tmp/base.json
```

## Export the graph

Bulk NDJSON streams, for ingesting the graph somewhere else.

| Command | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `snapshot` | The whole graph: header, files, external endpoints, symbols, relations, summary. Also supports `--format compact-ndjson`. |

---
title: review
description: Run a multi-agent review against the current branch and consolidate the results into a final verdict.
---

Run a multi-agent review against the current branch.

```bash
entire review [PROFILE] [flags]
```

`entire review` starts reviewer agents in parallel, then uses a judge agent to consolidate their reports into a final verdict.

Reviews are saved as named profiles in Entire settings. On first run, guided setup writes a profile and asks before starting agents.

## Configure a Review Profile

Open the review setup flow:

```bash
entire review --configure
```

Use non-interactive flags when you want to create or update a profile from a script:

```bash
entire review --configure \
  --set-agents codex,claude-code \
  --set-judge codex \
  --set-output local
```

This creates the default `general` profile unless you choose another profile name in the interactive setup.

## Run a Review

Run a named profile:

```bash
entire review general
```

You can also select a profile with `--profile`:

```bash
entire review --profile general
```

Scope the review against a specific base branch:

```bash
entire review general --base origin/main
```

Add one-off instructions for a single run:

```bash
entire review general --prompt "Focus on auth, error handling, and missing tests."
```

Run only one reviewer from the selected profile:

```bash
entire review general --agent codex
```

## Flags

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--configure` | Set up a review profile. Shows available agents and profiles unless paired with `--set-*` flags. |
| `--set-agents AGENTS` | With `--configure`, set comma-separated reviewer agents for the profile. |
| `--set-judge AGENT[=MODEL]` | With `--configure`, set the consolidating judge. |
| `--set-output local` | With `--configure`, deliver the verdict locally. Defaults to `local`. |
| `--local` | With `--configure`, save to `.entire/settings.local.json` instead of shared `.entire/settings.json`. |
| `--set-task TEXT` | With `--configure`, set the profile's canonical task text. |
| `--set-model AGENT=MODEL` | With `--configure`, set a model for a reviewer agent. Repeatable. |
| `--set-slot AGENT[=MODEL]` | With `--configure`, set one reviewer slot. Repeatable; the same agent or model can appear more than once. |
| `--edit` | Reopen the advanced review profile skill picker. |
| `--findings` | Browse local review findings. |
| `--agent NAME` | Run one reviewer from the selected profile. |
| `--agents` | List reviewer agents available for the selected profile. |
| `--model NAME` | Override the model for the selected `--agent` reviewer. Requires `--agent`. |
| `--models` | List the models each review agent advertises. Optionally combine with `--agent NAME`. |
| `--profile NAME` | Select a review profile. You can also pass the profile name as the positional argument. |
| `--prompt TEXT` | Add one-off instructions for this review run. |
| `--timeout DURATION` | Maximum time each reviewer may run before being marked failed. Defaults to `10m0s`; `0` disables the timeout. |
| `--base REF` | Scope the review against a Git ref instead of the default mainline ref. Defaults to the first existing ref from `origin/HEAD`, `origin/main`, `origin/master`, `main`, or `master`. |
| `--list` | List configured review profiles, reviewers, judges, and output modes. |
| `-h, --help` | Show help for `entire review`. |

<Note>
`entire review --findings` only browses local findings. It does not apply fixes.
</Note>

## Attach an Existing Review

To tag an already-finished session as a review, use [`entire session attach`](/cli-reference/attach) with `--review`:

```bash
entire session attach SESSION_ID --review
```

## Examples

```bash
# Configure a review profile
entire review --configure

# Configure a profile without the interactive setup
entire review --configure --set-agents codex,claude-code --set-judge codex --set-output local

# Run the general profile
entire review general

# Review a stacked branch against its parent
entire review general --base origin/my-parent-branch

# Run one configured reviewer
entire review general --agent codex

# Browse local findings
entire review --findings

# List configured profiles
entire review --list
```

Run a multi-agent investigation. Agents take turns appending findings, evidence, and analysis to a shared findings document until quorum is reached.

```bash
entire investigate [SEED_DOC] [flags]
```

---
title: Security & Privacy
description: Where your data lives, what's redacted before storage, how to add redaction rules, when data leaves your machine, and how to report security issues
---

Entire stores AI session transcripts as Git data alongside your code. Secret detection is built on [Betterleaks](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks), with additional Entire-specific layers for high-entropy strings, credentialed URIs, database connection strings, user-defined regex rules, and opt-in PII. This page explains what's stored, how secrets and PII are redacted before storage, how to add your own redaction rules, when data leaves your machine, how commits are signed, and how to report security issues.

<Note>
  Deleting your Entire account removes your account and profile data from Entire.
  It does not remove the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch from your own Git
  repository — delete that branch yourself. See [Delete your account](/delete-account).
</Note>

## Where your data lives

Transcripts and checkpoint metadata go to a dedicated branch in **your** Git repository (`entire/checkpoints/v1`), not to a service Entire controls. The web app at [entire.io](https://entire.io) reads from that branch — what users see in the web app is the *already-redacted* content from the branch.

Anyone with access to your repository can view the transcript branch. If your repository is public, that branch is public.

<Warning>
  Redaction is best-effort, not a guarantee. For sensitive workloads — customer data, internal credentials, regulated material — use a **private** repository.
</Warning>

<Tip>
  Starting in `v0.6.2`, Entire supports user-defined redaction: inline regex rules in settings and reusable rule packs under `.entire/redactors/`. See **User-defined redaction** below.
</Tip>

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please **do not** open a public GitHub issue for a security vulnerability.

<Card title="Email security@entire.io" icon="envelope" href="mailto:security@entire.io">
  Report security vulnerabilities directly. We acknowledge within 48 hours and aim to resolve criticals within 90 days. Full disclosure policy below.
</Card>

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Data storage details">
    **The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch** is the permanent home for redacted transcripts and checkpoint metadata. It's pushed alongside your code with normal `git push`. Anyone with access to your repository can read it.

    **Shadow branches** (`entire/<short-hash>`) hold working snapshots during a live session. Metadata (transcripts, prompts, incremental checkpoint data, subagent transcripts) is redacted on write. **Code-file snapshots, however, are raw blobs of your working tree without redaction** — so any hardcoded secrets in your source files appear unredacted on the shadow branch. Gitignored files (e.g. `.env`) are filtered out of those snapshots as a partial defense. Shadow branches are local-only and **are not pushed by Entire**; do not push them manually, because unredacted source content would land on the remote.

    **Two redaction passes for metadata.** Metadata is redacted on shadow-branch writes and again at condensation time when data is rolled into `entire/checkpoints/v1`. The metadata that lands in checkpoint storage — local or pushed — has been through redaction; the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch contains only metadata, no source code.

    **`RedactedBytes` type guarantee.** Internally, the redact package exposes a typed wrapper that compile-time enforces redaction has happened before checkpoint writes — accidental writes of un-redacted data are caught at the type level rather than at runtime.

    **Commit trailers.** Commits on your normal branches gain `Entire-Checkpoint: <12-char-hex>` and `Entire-Attribution: <percent> agent (<n>/<m> lines)` trailers. The trailers are public on push and live forever in commit messages. The hex is a random ID with no embedded PII; the attribution counts are aggregate numbers (no per-line content).

    **Remote URL redaction in logs.** When a fetch or push fails, error messages and `.entire/logs/` entries strip passwords from URLs (e.g. `REDACTED`) so credentials don't end up in local log files.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Secret redaction (always on)">
    Five built-in detection passes run during condensation. Anything matched by any built-in layer is replaced with the literal token `REDACTED`. The built-in secret pipeline cannot be disabled; user-defined rules and PII add configurable layers on top.

    1. **Entropy scoring.** Strings of 10+ alphanumeric characters with Shannon entropy above 4.5 are flagged. Catches API keys and tokens that don't match any known vendor pattern.
    2. **Pattern matching via Betterleaks.** The CLI embeds the [Betterleaks](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks) detector, which ships ~260+ rules covering cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure), version-control platforms (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), payment processors (Stripe, Square), communication tools (Slack, Discord, Twilio), private-key blocks (RSA, DSA, EC, PGP, OpenSSH), and generic credentials (bearer tokens, basic auth, JWTs).
    3. **Credentialed URI detection.** URLs that embed `user:password@host` — for example `REDACTED` or `REDACTED` — are redacted as a unit. These often have moderate entropy and aren't reliably caught by vendor-specific patterns.
    4. **Database connection-string detection.** Four sub-patterns: JDBC URIs (`jdbc:...`), database URLs (Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, Redis), Postgres-style keyword DSNs (`REDACTED), and SQL-Server-style semicolon connection strings (`REDACTED). When a real (non-placeholder) password is present, the entire connection string is redacted because partial fragments can still expose sensitive material.
    5. **Bounded credential value detection.** Variable assignments where the key matches a known credential name (`DB_PASSWORD`, `PGPASSWORD`, `MYSQL_PWD`, `REDIS_PASSWORD`, `MONGO_PASSWORD`, `MONGODB_PASSWORD`). Inside JSON, generic `password`/`passwd`/`pwd` keys are also redacted when the surrounding object looks like a connection descriptor — i.e. it contains both a host-like field (`host`/`hostname`/`server`/`addr`/`address`/`datasource`) and a user-like field (`user`/`username`/`userid`/`uid`). Only the value is redacted; the key is preserved.

    **False-positive handling:**

    - JSON fields named `signature` are skipped entirely.
    - JSON keys ending in `id` or `ids` are skipped (these are typically opaque identifiers).
    - JSON keys for structural paths (`filepath`, `file_path`, `cwd`, `root`, `directory`, `dir`, `path`) are skipped.
    - JSON objects with `type` starting with `image` or equal to `base64` are skipped (image and base64-encoded payloads are not scanned).
    - Placeholder values are not redacted. Detected by exact match (`changeme`, `example`, `placeholder`, `your_password`, `your_db_password`, `your_secret`, `secret_here`, plus prior `REDACTED`/`[REDACTED]`/`<REDACTED>` markers) **or** by shape: shell expansions like `${DB_PASSWORD}`, bracketed names like `<password>` or `<your-db-password>`, and mask runs of three or more `*`, `x`, `.`, or `-` (so `***`, `xxxx`, `....`, `----` all match).
    - Connection strings whose passwords are placeholders (e.g. `${DB_PASSWORD}`) are left intact.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="User-defined redaction">
    User-defined redaction lets teams add regex-based rules on top of Entire's built-in secret detection. Use it for internal token formats, project-specific identifiers, codenames, customer names, or other string patterns you do not want stored in session transcripts or checkpoint metadata.

    Custom rules use Go/RE2 regular expressions, so lookarounds and backreferences are not supported. Matches are replaced with the plain `REDACTED` token. Rule labels are for diagnostics only.

    **Inline rules.** For simple project-level rules, add `redaction.custom_redactions` to `.entire/settings.json`:

    ```json
    {
      "redaction": {
        "custom_redactions": {
          "acme_token": "ACME_TOKEN_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}",
          "internal_id": "INTERNAL_[a-z]{6}_[0-9]{4}"
        }
      }
    }
    ```

    For personal-only rules, put the same config in `.entire/settings.local.json`. Local settings merge with shared settings, so users can add private rules without changing team configuration.

    **Rule packs.** For reusable rules, place YAML or JSON packs under `.entire/redactors/`:

    ```yaml
    # .entire/redactors/acme-internal.yaml
    name: acme-internal
    version: 1.0.0
    description: Internal ACME service tokens
    rules:
      - id: acme-token
        description: Long-lived ACME service tokens
        regex: 'ACME_TOKEN_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}'
        samples:
          - { input: "REDACTED", redacted: true }
          - { input: "ACME_TOKEN_short", redacted: false }

      - id: acme-session
        regex: 'asess_[a-f0-9]{32}'
    ```

    Required fields: `name` (must match the filename stem), `version`, and one or more `rules`, each with a unique `id` and a `regex`. Pack names and rule IDs may contain letters, numbers, `.`, `_`, and `-`. Supported extensions are `.yaml`, `.yml`, and `.json`.

    **Personal rule packs.** Put uncommitted packs under `.entire/redactors/local/`. `entire enable` keeps that path ignored so personal codenames, customer references, or local-only patterns do not become shared repo configuration.

    **Self-tests.** Rules can include `samples` with `{ input, redacted }` expectations. Entire checks samples when it loads the pack. A failing sample logs a warning but does not disable the rule.

    **When rules take effect.** No separate command is required. Entire loads inline rules and rule packs on the next CLI or hook invocation. Invalid regexes or malformed packs are skipped and logged instead of crashing the CLI.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="PII redaction (optional)">
    PII redaction is a separate, **opt-in** layer that runs in addition to secret redaction. Disabled by default. Configured under `redaction.pii` in `.entire/settings.json` (team-shared) or `.entire/settings.local.json` (personal, gitignored).

    **Built-in categories:**

    | Category | Default when PII is enabled | Replacement token |
    |---|---|---|
    | `email` | On | `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` |
    | `phone` | On | `[REDACTED_PHONE]` |
    | `address` (US street addresses) | Off (more false-positive prone) | `[REDACTED_ADDRESS]` |

    **Email allowlist.** These addresses are *not* redacted as PII because they're public bot/CI metadata that appear in nearly every git transcript: `noreply@*`, `actions@*`, `*@users.noreply.github.com`, `*@noreply.github.com`.

    **Custom patterns.** Teams can add their own regex patterns via `custom_patterns`. The label becomes part of the replacement token (uppercased). For example, `{"employee_id": "EMP-\\d{6}"}` produces `[REDACTED_EMPLOYEE_ID]`.

    **Settings example:**

    ```json
    {
      "redaction": {
        "pii": {
          "enabled": true,
          "email": true,
          "phone": true,
          "address": false,
          "custom_patterns": {
            "employee_id": "EMP-\\d{6}"
          }
        }
      }
    }
    ```

    **Where to put custom patterns.** Patterns added under `redaction.pii.custom_patterns` in `.entire/settings.json` are committed to the repo and shared with the team — useful for org-wide rules, but the regex itself becomes public if the repo is public. For patterns that themselves shouldn't leak (e.g. a regex that reveals an internal ID format), add them to `.entire/settings.local.json` (gitignored, personal) instead.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Limitations of redaction">
    - **Best-effort.** Novel or low-entropy secrets (short passwords, predictable tokens) may not be caught.
    - **Filenames and binary data.** Secrets in filenames, binary files, or deeply nested structures may not be detected.
    - **Skip rules can hide secrets.** The structural-field and image/base64 skip rules trade detection coverage for false-positive avoidance — a secret embedded in a `path` field or a base64 blob will not be redacted.
    - **Custom rules are user-authored.** Teams own the correctness of their `custom_redactions`, rule packs, and PII `custom_patterns`. Invalid regexes are logged and skipped, not enforced.
    - **Custom redaction does not scrub source snapshots.** It applies to transcript, prompt, and checkpoint metadata content written by Entire. Temporary checkpoint branches can still contain raw source-file snapshots, so hardcoded secrets should be avoided entirely.
    - **Users are ultimately responsible** for reviewing what they push. Redaction is a safety net, not a guarantee.

title: Mirrors
sidebarTitle: Overview
description: Connect an existing GitHub repository to Entire with an Entire-backed Git remote.
---

## What is a mirror?

A mirror is a synced, read-optimized copy of a GitHub repository, hosted on Entire's Git network in the region you choose. The repository stays on GitHub, and mirroring gives developers and agents a low-latency `entire://` remote they can clone, fetch, and push through without a hard cutover.

Developers can keep pushing to GitHub as usual, while agents, automation, or selected users use the `entire://` remote. Behind the scenes, Entire keeps the mirror in sync.

Mirrors are served by the same distributed network as [Entire Repositories](/guides/repositories/overview). See that page for the larger model behind regional Git reads, repository state, and agent traffic.

## How mirrors work

To mirror a GitHub repository, the [Entire GitHub App must be able to access the repository](/guides/repositories/github-app-access). After that, a user with access to the GitHub repository can create the mirror from Entire.io or sign in with `entire login` and create it from the CLI.

When the mirror is created:

- Entire syncs the repository from GitHub
- the mirror is placed in the selected Entire region
- users get an `entire://` Git remote
- agents can clone and fetch from the regional mirror
- pushes through the mirror are authenticated with GitHub

The mirror keeps Git reads close to where agents run, while pushes remain authenticated with GitHub.

## Create a mirror

To create a mirror from the web app, see [Mirrors in Entire.io](/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-entire-io).

For the command-line flow, see [Mirrors in CLI](/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-cli). For an end-to-end tutorial, see [Mirror a GitHub Repository](/learn/mirror-a-github-repository).

## What changes

Creating a mirror gives you:

- a synced Entire copy of the GitHub repository
- an `entire://` remote for Git operations
- a regional read path for agents and automation
- an Entire mirror access list synced hourly with GitHub collaborators

You can use the mirror from a fresh clone or add it as a remote to an existing checkout.

## What does not change

Creating a mirror does not:

- move, delete, or replace the GitHub repository
- require every developer to change remotes
- rewrite Git history
- bypass GitHub authentication for pushes

Entire syncs GitHub collaborators into mirror access hourly. See [Mirror Access and Permissions](/guides/repositories/mirror-access-and-permissions) for GitHub-synced access, self-onboarding, and offboarding.

## Unmirrored branches

Branches whose names start with `entire/unmirrored/` are never synced to GitHub. An unmirrored branch exists only in the Entire region you push it to: it does not appear on GitHub, and it is not available from mirrors in other regions.

Because pushes to unmirrored branches stay in Entire instead of being forwarded to GitHub, they are not subject to GitHub's push rate limits. Use an unmirrored branch when you need:

- more push throughput than GitHub allows
- a branch you can keep pushing to while GitHub is unavailable
- a target for push benchmarks

To benchmark push throughput, for example with [ForgeMark](https://github.com/entireio/forgemark), Entire's open-source Git push benchmarking tool, push to an unmirrored branch. Pushes to regular branches are forwarded to GitHub, so a benchmark against them measures GitHub's push rate limits rather than Entire's throughput.

Mirror access still applies: you need write access through the mirror to push an unmirrored branch. To publish the work on GitHub later, push the same commits to a branch name outside the `entire/unmirrored/` prefix.

<Warning>
Entire does not currently back up unmirrored branches. Keep a copy of any work you cannot afford to lose on a mirrored branch or on GitHub.
</Warning>

## Limitations

Mirrors do not currently support Git LFS. See [Limitations](/guides/repositories/limitations) for details and workarounds.

title: import
description: Import pre-existing local agent transcripts as read-only checkpoints.
---

Import pre-existing local agent transcripts for the current repository as read-only checkpoints.

```bash
entire import AGENT [flags]
```

<Note>
`entire import` is experimental and hidden from the top-level help in Entire CLI `0.7.8`. Run `entire import --help` to see the agents supported by your installed CLI version.
</Note>

## Supported agents

In Entire CLI `0.7.8`, import supports:

| Agent | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `entire import claude-code` |
| Codex | `entire import codex` |
| Copilot CLI | `entire import copilot-cli` |
| Cursor | `entire import cursor` |
| Factory | `entire import factoryai-droid` |
| Gemini CLI | `entire import gemini` |
| Pi | `entire import pi` |

## Flags

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--dry-run` | Report what would be imported without writing checkpoints |
| `--path DIRECTORY` | Override the transcript directory to import from |
| `--session ID` | Import only this session ID. Repeatable. |

## Examples

Check what would be imported:

```bash
entire import claude-code --dry-run
```

Import Claude Code transcript history:

```bash
entire import claude-code
```

title: activity
description: Show your Entire activity overview from your hosted Entire account.
---

Show your Entire activity overview from your hosted Entire account.

```bash
entire activity
```

This command loads your activity from the last month from [entire.io](https://entire.io), including:

- Activity overview and aggregate stats
- Repository breakdown
- Recent commits from the last month, grouped by day

If you are not logged in, authenticate first:

```bash
entire login
```

When you run `entire activity` in an interactive terminal, it opens a richer terminal UI. In non-interactive contexts, such as piped output, or when accessibility mode is enabled with `ACCESSIBLE=1`, it falls back to a simpler static text view that works better with screen readers.

```bash
# Open the interactive activity view
entire activity

# Use simpler static output for screen readers
ACCESSIBLE=1 entire activity
```

<Note>
`entire activity` shows account-level activity from Entire, not just local repository state.
</Note>

Read through the Entire docs in `/Users/lizziesiegle/Desktop/entire-os/docs` (nav in `docs.json`, plus the guides, CLI reference, agents, and learn tabs). No files touched. Here's a content slate, grouped like a season schedule rather than one long rally.

## 1. Foundations (short, high-volume top-of-funnel)

| Topic | Angle | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| "Git shows what changed. Entire shows why." | 90-second explainer: the diff loses the prompt, the files inspected, the tools run, the decisions | `overview.mdx` |
| First checkpoint in 5 minutes | Install, `entire enable -y --agent claude-code`, prompt, commit, `entire checkpoint list` | `quickstart.mdx` |
| Where your data actually lives | The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch in *your* repo, working branch stays clean, no extra commits | `quickstart.mdx`, `security.mdx` |
| Stable vs nightly channels | Homebrew cask, install script `--channel nightly`, Scoop is stable-only, `entire version` | `installation.mdx`, `updating.mdx` |
| Entire CLI vs Entire.io | Which surface for which job | `platforms/*` |
| Vocabulary video | Session, checkpoint, session context, shadow branch, trailer, mirror | `glossary.mdx` |

## 2. The provenance trilogy (your strongest hook)

- **`entire blame`**: git blame with `AI` / `MX` / `HU` tags per line, then `--long` for agent, model, author, and session columns.
- **`entire why src/app.ts:21`**: jump from one line to the commit, checkpoint, prompt, and session behind it.
- **`entire investigate`**: multi-agent investigation from a prompt, seed doc, or `--issue-link`, agents appending findings until quorum, then `investigate fix RUN_ID` to hand findings to a coding agent as grounded context.
- **Capstone**: "I found a weird line of code in a repo I didn't write" walkthrough, straight off `learn/investigate-why-code-exists.mdx`.

## 3. Checkpoints in depth

- What triggers a checkpoint, and the commit-time prompt ("link this commit to session context? Y/n/always").
- Three storage strategies, one video each: with your code, in a separate repo, or fully local. Good "which one is right for your team" comparison.
- `entire checkpoint explain` for an AI explanation of a session or commit.
- `entire checkpoint rewind` (the "undo the agent's last three moves" video, mind the warning in the docs).
- Reviewing checkpoints in the CLI vs in Entire.io, side by side.
- Why commit trailers instead of Git notes, and why there's no durable line-level attribution. The FAQ is two spicy engineering-decision answers that make a great "under the hood" episode.

## 4. Sessions and continuity

- `entire session resume` with no args: interactive picker across worktrees, checks out the branch, restores the session log, offers to start the agent.
- `entire session attach` for work the agent did outside capture, plus `--review` to tag a finished session as a review.
- `entire import claude-code --dry-run` then real: retroactively pull months of existing local transcripts in as read-only checkpoints. This is a *very* good video, because most viewers already have that history sitting on disk.
- `entire session stop` / `entire doctor` for stuck sessions.
- Inspecting token usage per session from the CLI.

## 5. Graph (best "wow" demo in the docs)

- Why your agent greps three times and still misses the file, and what a ranked `file:line` query replaces.
- Setup: `entire plugin install graph`, `entire graph init-agents --repo .`, the three managed files, and the detail people will miss: commit them, because Graph disables cache reuse on a dirty tree so every query rebuilds.
- `entire graph impact --symbol Router.Match`: blast radius, direct and transitive callers, type consumers, co-change files. "What breaks if I change this?"
- `go test ./... 2>&1 | entire graph explain`: pipe a failing test into the graph and get the declarations back.
- `entire graph verify` with `--record-baseline`, so pre-existing failures get labeled `PRE-EXISTING` instead of blamed on your change.
- `entire graph search` vs `entire search`: same word, different questions. The docs have a ready-made comparison table.
- Honest-limits episode: static analysis is best effort, interfaces and reflection get missed, 36 languages semantic plus 149 inventory-only, check with `entire graph capabilities --json`.

## 6. Multi-agent workflows

- `entire review --configure --set-agents codex,claude-code --set-judge codex`: reviewers in parallel, a judge consolidating a verdict. Cross-agent review is a genuinely novel demo.
- Review profiles as committed team config vs `--local` personal overrides, plus `--base origin/parent-branch` for stacked branches.
- `entire recap --week --view team`: interactive activity summary by time window and agent.
- `entire dispatch`: turn recent agent work into a shareable markdown update for a standup or a non-technical stakeholder.
- `entire activity` for account-level stats, including the `ACCESSIBLE=1` static mode.
- `entire labs` as the "what's cooking" discovery command.

## 7. Skills (make your agent use Entire for you)

One video per skill is eleven videos, or bundle them:

- Install paths: Claude Code plugin marketplace, `npx skills add`, `gemini extensions install`, or a plain clone for Codex.
- Provenance trio: `explain`, `what-happened`, `replay`.
- Memory trio: `search`, `recall`, `teach`.
- Handoff pair: `session-handoff` and `session-crosslink`. "Hand off this session" from Claude Code to Codex is a killer 60-second short.
- `session-to-skill`: turn a session you just finished into a reusable skill. Meta and very shareable.

## 8. Search

- Semantic search over commits and sessions vs `--code` for literal text across indexed repos.
- Searching from inside your agent via the search skill: "have we done this before?"
- Search in the browser: Commits, Sessions, and Code tabs.

## 9. Repos, mirrors, and scale

- Mirror a GitHub repo without a cutover: `entire://` remote, GitHub stays source of truth, hourly collaborator sync.
- Regional data residency choice at mirror creation.
- `entire/unmirrored/` branches: never synced to GitHub, not subject to GitHub push rate limits, plus the ForgeMark benchmark angle. Also the warning that they aren't backed up.
- Limitations episode: no Git LFS, and the workarounds.

## 10. Config, privacy, security (the trust-building tier)

- Settings layers: `.entire/settings.json` committed vs `.entire/settings.local.json` personal, and which generated files belong in Git.
- Git hooks and agent hooks: what `entire enable` actually installed on your machine.
- Redaction deep dive: five always-on passes (entropy over 4.5, ~260 Betterleaks patterns, credentialed URIs, DB connection strings, bounded credential values), and the false-positive skips.
- Write your own redaction rules: inline `custom_redactions`, YAML rule packs under `.entire/redactors/` with self-testing `samples`, and personal packs under `redactors/local/`.
- Opt-in PII redaction, and the sharp point that a regex in shared settings becomes public if the repo is public.
- The shadow-branch caveat, worth its own honest video: shadow branches hold *raw* source snapshots, are local-only, and should never be pushed manually.
- Deleting your account does not delete the checkpoints branch from your repo.

## 11. Builder tier (small audience, high credibility)

- Write an external agent plugin: drop an executable named `entire-agent-<name>` on `$PATH` and the CLI auto-discovers it. Cover the lifecycle, required commands, and data model.
- Agent support matrix as a comparison video: Claude Code has nested subagent capture, Cursor has no rewind or resume, Gemini captures files but limited transcript, OpenCode supports mid-turn commits.
- `--json` everywhere: script `blame`, `why`, and graph output into your own dashboards.

## 12. Tips-and-tricks shorts (fast to produce, good retention)

1. Type `always` at the commit prompt once, never answer it again.
2. `entire import claude-code --dry-run` on a repo you've used for months.
3. Commit the Graph files or every query pays full index cost.
4. `entire graph search --profile full`, because the default is `fast` and `full` is what activates the call graph.
5. `entire recap --static --color never` for pasting into Slack or a PR.
6. `entire doctor` before you debug anything else.
7. `entire review general --agent codex` when you want one reviewer, not the whole panel.
8. `entire blame FILE --line 12-20 --long`.
9. `entire agent add NAME` to capture a second agent in the same repo.
10. `entire graph impact` before touching any shared function.

## Series framing ideas

- **"Why does this code exist?"** A recurring format: pick a real open-source line, trace it with blame → why → investigate. Repeatable forever.
- **"Two agents, one repo."** Cross-agent handoff and cross-agent review, which is the part no other tool does.
- **"Ship it Saturday."** Build a small feature start to finish, then show the checkpoint trail as the receipt.

Two notes on overlap: the docs already have one video tutorial page (`learn/videos/enable-entire.mdx`) plus embedded Cloudflare Stream clips on the skills, search, resume, and agents pages, so those four have existing footage you can extend rather than duplicate. And `investigate`, `import`, and `review` are all flagged experimental or lab-stage in the docs, so pin the CLI version on screen. Nothing worse than a tutorial that ages out mid-set.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Chicago-style heading pass for Entire docs.

Titles (frontmatter title/sidebarTitle, and H1 in bare .md files) -> CMOS 8.159
headline style. Subheads (H2-H6, plus H1 in .mdx where frontmatter supplies the
title) -> CMOS 8.158 sentence style.

Protected: fenced code blocks, inline code spans, links' target URLs, acronyms,
CamelCase identifiers, flags, filenames, and the proper-noun lexicon below.
"""
import re
import sys
import pathlib

# --- lexicon -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Proper nouns that keep their capitalization in sentence-style subheads.
PROPER = {
    # Entire and its surfaces
    "Entire", "Entire.io", "ForgeMark", "Betterleaks", "Graph", "Skill", "Skills",
    # agents and vendors
    "Claude", "Code", "Codex", "Copilot", "Cursor", "Factory", "Droid", "Gemini",
    "OpenCode", "Pi", "Anthropic", "Google", "GitHub", "GitLab", "Bitbucket",
    "Git", "Homebrew", "Scoop", "Mintlify", "Vite", "Slack", "Discord", "Twilio",
    "Stripe", "Square", "Postgres", "PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "MariaDB", "MongoDB",
    "Redis", "Docker", "Zscaler", "Cloudflare",
    # platforms and languages
    "macOS", "Linux", "Windows", "Unix", "Go", "Python", "TypeScript",
    "JavaScript", "Markdown", "YAML", "JSON", "Shannon",
    # tools of art that are capitalized in the prose
    "Chicago",
}
# Words that stay lowercase in headline style: articles, coordinating
# conjunctions, prepositions (CMOS 8.159), and infinitival "to".
HEADLINE_LOWER = {
    "a", "an", "the",
    "and", "but", "or", "nor", "for", "so", "yet",
    "about", "above", "across", "after", "against", "along", "among", "around",
    "as", "at", "before", "behind", "below", "beneath", "beside", "between",
    "beyond", "by", "despite", "down", "during", "except", "from", "in",
    "inside", "into", "like", "near", "of", "off", "on", "onto", "out",
    "outside", "over", "past", "per", "since", "than", "through", "throughout",
    "to", "toward", "under", "until", "up", "upon", "via", "with", "within",
    "without",
}
# Particles that stay capitalized when they belong to a phrasal verb.
PHRASAL_VERBS = {
    "set", "turn", "log", "sign", "back", "check", "clean", "hand", "look",
    "pick", "roll", "shut", "start", "opt", "fill", "bring", "hold", "keep",
    "push", "pull", "drop", "break", "carry", "catch", "clear", "cut", "figure",
}
PARTICLES = {"up", "on", "off", "out", "in", "down", "over", "through", "away", "back"}

TOKEN = re.compile(r"`[^`]*`|\[[^\]]*\]\([^)]*\)|[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9''\.\-/]*|[^A-Za-z`\[]+")


def is_protected_word(w):
    """Acronyms, identifiers, flags, filenames, versions keep their shape."""
    core = w.strip("()[],.:;\"'")
    if not core:
        return True
    if core in PROPER:
        return True
    if core.startswith("-"):            # --flag
        return True
    if core.upper() == core and len(core) > 1 and any(c.isalpha() for c in core):
        return True                     # CLI, API, PII, JSON, LFS, ID
    if any(c.isupper() for c in core[1:]):
        return True                     # CamelCase, Entire.io, macOS, NDJSON
    if "." in core or "/" in core or "_" in core:
        return True                     # filenames, paths, snake_case
    if any(c.isdigit() for c in core):
        return True
    return False


def split_tokens(text):
    return TOKEN.findall(text)


def sentence_case(text):
    """CMOS 8.158: capitalize the first word and proper nouns only."""
    out = []
    seen_word = False
    for tok in split_tokens(text):
        if tok.startswith("`") or tok.startswith("["):
            out.append(tok)
            if tok.startswith("`"):
                seen_word = True
            continue
        if not re.match(r"[A-Za-z]", tok):
            out.append(tok)
            continue
        core = tok
        if is_protected_word(core):
            out.append(core)
            seen_word = True
            continue
        if not seen_word:
            out.append(core[0].upper() + core[1:].lower())
        else:
            out.append(core.lower())
        seen_word = True
    return "".join(out)


def headline_case(text):
    """CMOS 8.159: first and last word plus all major words capitalized."""
    toks = split_tokens(text)
    word_idx = [i for i, t in enumerate(toks) if re.match(r"[A-Za-z]", t) and not t.startswith("`") and not t.startswith("[")]
    if not word_idx:
        return text
    first, last = word_idx[0], word_idx[-1]
    out = list(toks)
    prev_word = None
    for i in word_idx:
        tok = toks[i]
        if is_protected_word(tok):
            prev_word = tok.lower()
            continue
        low = tok.lower()
        cap = True
        if low in HEADLINE_LOWER and i not in (first, last):
            cap = False
            # phrasal-verb particles stay capitalized: "Set Up", "Turn On"
            if low in PARTICLES and prev_word in PHRASAL_VERBS:
                cap = True
        out[i] = (tok[0].upper() + tok[1:]) if cap else low
        prev_word = low
    return "".join(out)


FENCE = re.compile(r"^\s*(```|~~~)")


def process(path, apply=False):
    src = pathlib.Path(path).read_text()
    lines = src.split("\n")
    is_mdx = path.endswith(".mdx")
    out = []
    in_fence = False
    in_fm = False
    fm_done = False
    changes = []
    seen_h1 = False
    for n, line in enumerate(lines):
        new = line
        if n == 0 and line.strip() == "---" and not fm_done:
            in_fm = True
            out.append(line)
            continue
        if in_fm:
            if line.strip() == "---":
                in_fm = False
                fm_done = True
                out.append(line)
                continue
            m = re.match(r"^(title|sidebarTitle):\s*(.*)$", line)
            if m:
                key, val = m.group(1), m.group(2).strip()
                quote = ""
                if val[:1] in "\"'" and val[-1:] == val[:1] and len(val) > 1:
                    quote, val = val[0], val[1:-1]
                fixed = headline_case(val)
                if fixed != val:
                    new = f"{key}: {quote}{fixed}{quote}"
            out.append(new)
            if new != line:
                changes.append((n + 1, line, new))
            continue
        if FENCE.match(line):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            out.append(line)
            continue
        if in_fence:
            out.append(line)
            continue
        m = re.match(r"^(#{1,6})\s+(.*?)\s*$", line)
        if m:
            hashes, text = m.group(1), m.group(2)
            level = len(hashes)
            if level == 1 and not is_mdx and not seen_h1:
                fixed = headline_case(text)   # bare .md H1 is the doc title
                seen_h1 = True
            else:
                fixed = sentence_case(text)
            if fixed != text:
                new = f"{hashes} {fixed}"
        out.append(new)
        if new != line:
            changes.append((n + 1, line, new))
    if apply and changes:
        pathlib.Path(path).write_text("\n".join(out))
    return changes


if __name__ == "__main__":
    apply = "--apply" in sys.argv
    paths = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")]
    total = 0
    for p in paths:
        ch = process(p, apply)
        if ch:
            print(f"\n=== {p}")
            for n, old, new in ch:
                print(f"  {n}: - {old}")
                print(f"  {n}: + {new}")
            total += len(ch)
    print(f"\n{total} heading/title lines {'changed' if apply else 'would change'} across {len(paths)} files")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Down-style common nouns in prose (CMOS 8.1).

The docs already lowercase these overwhelmingly mid-sentence; this pass fixes
the minority that were capitalized. Left alone: sentence and cell starts, link
text and component titles (which cite page names), headings, frontmatter,
code, and hyphenated identifiers such as Entire-Checkpoint.
"""
import re
import sys
import pathlib

TERMS = re.compile(
    r"(?<![\w`/\-.])"
    r"(Checkpoints|Checkpoint|Sessions|Session|Repositories|Repository|"
    r"Agents|Agent|Mirrors|Mirror|Dispatches|Dispatch)"
    r"(?![\w\-])"
)
FENCE = re.compile(r"^\s*(```|~~~)")
# spans whose contents cite a title and must keep their capitals
PROTECT = re.compile(r"`[^`]*`|\[[^\]]*\]|<[^>]+>|\{[^}]*\}")
SENTENCE_START = re.compile(r"(^|[.!?]\s+|\|\s*|^\s*[-*+>]\s*|\*\*|\d\.\s+|:\s+)$")


def fix_line(line):
    saved = []

    def hide(m):
        saved.append(m.group(0))
        return f"\x01{len(saved)-1}\x01"

    work = PROTECT.sub(hide, line)
    out = []
    pos = 0
    for m in TERMS.finditer(work):
        before = work[:m.start()]
        out.append(work[pos:m.start()])
        if SENTENCE_START.search(before) or before.rstrip().endswith(("**", "*", "#", '"')):
            out.append(m.group(1))
        else:
            out.append(m.group(1).lower())
        pos = m.end()
    out.append(work[pos:])
    work = "".join(out)
    return re.sub(r"\x01(\d+)\x01", lambda m: saved[int(m.group(1))], work)


def process(path, apply=False):
    lines = pathlib.Path(path).read_text().split("\n")
    out, changes = [], []
    in_fence = False
    in_fm = lines and lines[0].strip() == "---"
    for n, line in enumerate(lines):
        if in_fm:
            out.append(line)
            if n > 0 and line.strip() == "---":
                in_fm = False
            continue
        if FENCE.match(line):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            out.append(line)
            continue
        if in_fence or line.startswith("#"):
            out.append(line)
            continue
        new = fix_line(line)
        out.append(new)
        if new != line:
            changes.append((n + 1, line, new))
    if apply and changes:
        pathlib.Path(path).write_text("\n".join(out))
    return changes


if __name__ == "__main__":
    apply = "--apply" in sys.argv
    total = 0
    for p in [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")]:
        ch = process(p, apply)
        if ch:
            print(f"\n=== {p}")
            for n, old, new in ch:
                print(f"  {n}: - {old.strip()[:170]}")
                print(f"  {n}: + {new.strip()[:170]}")
            total += len(ch)
    print(f"\n{total} lines {'changed' if apply else 'would change'}")

content.text:
Done. Both trees are now in Chicago style, and every change is line-for-line (no content added or removed).

**What changed: 118 files, 904 lines** (93 in `docs/`, 25 in `entire-graph/docs/`). `AGENTS.md` in entire-graph was already modified before I started; I did not touch it.

Applied per your two decisions, plus the rest of the CMOS checklist:

- **Headline style for titles (CMOS 8.159)**, sentence style for subheads (8.158): 397 heading and title lines. Hyphenated compounds follow 8.161 (`Committed-Tree Cache Key`), with the prefix exception (`Non-zero`, `Multi-agent`).
- **Em dashes: 337 gone, zero left.** Chicago closes them up, but your no-em-dash rule wins, so each was rewritten into the punctuation the sentence wanted: a colon before an explanation, a comma before a conjunction, a period between two independent clauses, parentheses for asides. Six were shell comments inside code fences, covered because your rule includes code comments.
- **Component titles (141):** Accordion and Step titles read as subheads, so sentence style; Card and Tab titles cite page names, so headline style. Cards pointing at `/cli-reference/` and titles holding an email address kept their literal text.
- **Ampersands to "and"** (CMOS 6.21): the `Security and Privacy` page title plus the five links citing it, and three archive headings with their table-of-contents anchors updated to match.
- **Down style for common nouns** (8.1): 26 stray capitals on checkpoint, session, repository, agent, mirror, dispatch. This follows the docs' own dominant usage (485 lowercase to 48 capitalized for "checkpoint"), so it is not a new house style. Left capitalized: `Skill(s)` (44 to 13 the other way), `Graph` as the product name in the public docs, UI labels ("the Sessions tab", "Settings > Repository"), the glossary's defined terms, and page-name citations in link text.
- **Numbers:** CMOS 9.3's technical rule (spell out zero through nine) rather than 9.2, since these docs are thick with flags and measurements. Seven prose counts spelled out ("up to five repositories"); labels, specs, ranges, and measurements keep numerals. One sentence opening with "36" was reworded per 9.5.
- **`e.g.`/`i.e.` now take a following comma** (6.51): 14 lines. Serial commas were already near-perfect: only two genuine violations existed, both fixed.

**Verification:** your running `mint dev` caught two real breakages I introduced, where a colon replacing an em dash inside an unquoted YAML `description:` broke the frontmatter in `agents/overview.mdx` and `web/troubleshooting.mdx`. Both rewritten without colons and confirmed reprocessing cleanly. I also scanned all 135 frontmatter blocks for the same hazard (zero remaining), checked that code fences, inline-code spans, bold markers, link counts, and line counts are byte-identical in structure across all 118 files, and validated every internal anchor link.

Three things worth your eyes, none of them mine:

1. Five anchor links in `docs/` were already broken at HEAD (identical before and after my pass), all pointing into `guides/configuration/`: `checkpoint-storage#checkpoint-remote`, `#keep-checkpoints-local`, `#store-checkpoints-with-your-code`, `agent-hooks#external-agent-plugins`, `settings-layers#project-settings-file`.
2. Three table-of-contents links in `entire-graph/docs/archive/2026-08-12-legacy-details.md` point at headings that no longer exist (`#️-language-support`, `#️-architecture`, `#️-current-limits`).
3. The graph guide pages were rewritten on disk earlier today by someone else, so `guides/graph/overview.mdx` is now the short "Benefits of using entire-graph" version rather than the longer one I read yesterday. I styled what is currently on disk.

Two judgment calls I made rather than asking: CLI-reference page titles and all-lowercase headings like `## graph search` stay lowercase, because they are literal command names rather than prose, and `Search` capitalization was left as authored, since it names a UI page in Entire.io about a third of the time and normalizing it would have been a guess.
